'''Daniel George Nocera''' (born July 3, 1957) is an American [[chemist]], currently the Patterson Rockwood Professor of Energy in the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="Colen" /> He is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. In 2006 he was described as a "major force in the field of inorganic photochemistry and photophysics".<ref name="APS2006" /> ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine included him in its 2009 list of the 100 most influential people.<ref name="Krupp">{{Cite news
 | title = The 2009 Time 100: Daniel Nocera
 | last1 = Krupp | first1 = Fred
 | magazine = [[Time (magazine)|Time]]
 | url = https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,1894410_1893209_1893470,00.html
 | date = April 30, 2009 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="bbc">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p01g94yj|title=The Future of Renewable Energy|publisher=[[BBC World Service]] |year=2013|quote=How do we develop a practical, reliable, cheap and globally relevant supply of renewable energy and improve on the meagre 10% of our power needs which renewables currently provide? Quentin Cooper travels to the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]'s Challenges in Chemical Renewable Energy meeting in Cambridge, UK, to hear about ideas and latest research results from Brazilian authority on bioenergy [[Carlos Henrique de Brito Cruz]], Cambridge University's creator of better batteries [[Clare Grey]], Harvard pioneer of artificial photosynthesis Daniel Nocera and research director of the UK Energy Research Centre Jim Watson.}}</ref>

Nocera has opened up new areas of basic research into the mechanisms of energy conversion in biology and chemistry, including the study of multielectron excited states and [[proton coupled electron transfer]] (PCET). He works on research applications in [[artificial photosynthesis]] and [[solar fuel]]s, including an "artificial leaf" that mimics [[photosynthesis]] in plants.<ref name="Hall" /> In 2009, Nocera formed Sun Catalytix, a startup for development of the artificial leaf.  The company was bought by Lockheed Martin in 2014.

== Early life and education ==
Daniel George Nocera was born July 3, 1957, in [[Medford, Massachusetts]]. He graduated from [[Bergenfield High School]], [[Bergenfield, New Jersey]], in 1975.<ref name="Hall">{{Cite journal
 | title = Daniel Nocera: Maverick Inventor of the Artificial Leaf
 | last1 = Hall | first1 = Stephen S.
 | journal = National Geographic
 | url = http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/innovators/2014/05/140519-nocera-chemistry-artificial-leaf-solar-renewable-energy/
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140521124402/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/innovators/2014/05/140519-nocera-chemistry-artificial-leaf-solar-renewable-energy/
 | url-status = dead
 | archive-date = May 21, 2014
 | date = May 19, 2014
}}</ref>

Nocera attended [[Rutgers University]], where he worked with Lester R. Morss and Joseph Potenza.<ref name="Nair">{{Cite journal
 | title = Profile of Daniel G. Nocera
 | last1 = Nair | first1 = P.
 | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
 | year = 2012 | volume = 109 | issue = 1 | pages = 15–17
 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1118655109 | pmc = 3252940 | pmid = 22219319
 | bibcode = 2012PNAS..109...15N| doi-access = free }}</ref> Nocera received a B.S. degree in [[chemistry]] from Rutgers University in 1979.<ref name="Pepling" />

He then attended the [[California Institute of Technology]], where he received a [[PhD]] in chemistry in 1984<ref>{{cite thesis|url=https://thesis.library.caltech.edu/429/|title=Spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and photochemistry of polynuclear metal-metal bonded complexes|last=Nocera|first=Daniel George|date=March 4, 1984|website=thesis.library.caltech.edu|publisher=California Institute of Technology|type=phd}}</ref> for his work with Professor [[Harry B. Gray]] on the ''[[Spectroscopy]], [[Electrochemistry]], and [[Photochemistry]] of Polynuclear Metal-Metal Bonded Complexes''.<ref>{{Cite thesis
 | title = Spectroscopy, Electrochemistry, and Photochemistry of Polynuclear Metal-Metal Bonded Complexes
 | last = Nocera | first = Daniel George
 | publisher = [[Caltech]]
 | url = http://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechETD:etd-02012005-160716
 | type = Abstract
 | date = August 16, 1983 | access-date = August 3, 2008
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web
 | title = CU Energy Initiative/NREL Symposium – Keynote Speakers
 | publisher = [[University of Colorado at Boulder]] / [[National Renewable Energy Laboratory]] (NREL)
 | url = http://ei.colorado.edu/events/fall_2006_symposium/keynote_address.html
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080312172733/http://ei.colorado.edu/events/fall_2006_symposium/keynote_address.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive -->
 | date = October 3, 2006 | access-date = August 3, 2008 | archive-date = March 12, 2008
}}</ref> His work with Gray included the first experimental examination of [[electron transfer]] in [[ruthenium]]-modified proteins, since considered "a hallmark of research on protein electron transfer".<ref name="APS2006" />

== Career and research ==
Nocera joined the faculty of [[Michigan State University]] in 1984<ref name="Hall" /> as assistant professor, and became a full professor at MSU in 1990.<ref name="MSU1999" />

He moved to [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a professor of chemistry in 1997,<ref name="MSU1999">{{Cite web
 |title        = Nineteenth Annual Dow/Karabatsos Distinguished Lectureship presents Prof. Daniel G. Nocera
 |publisher    = Michigan State University
 |url          = http://www.cem.msu.edu/lecture_dk_1999.html
 |access-date  = April 5, 2016
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20091030041044/http://www.cem.msu.edu/lecture_dk_1999.html
 |archive-date = October 30, 2009
 |url-status   = dead
 |df           = mdy-all
}}</ref> serving as the W. M. Keck Professor of Energy (2002–2007) and the Henry Dreyfus Professor of Energy (2007–2013).<ref name="Frontiers">{{cite web|title=Curricula Vitae of Principal Investigators|url=http://www.cngmd-efrc.org/cv.html#nocera|website=Center for Next-Generation of Materials by Design: An Energy Frontier Research Center|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref> He was director of the Solar Revolution Project at MIT, founded in 2008.<ref name="LaMonica2008">{{Cite news
 | title = MIT says it wants a solar 'revolution'
 | last1 = LaMonica | first1 = Martin
 | work = CNET
 | url = http://www.cnet.com/news/mit-says-it-wants-a-solar-revolution/
 | date = April 22, 2008 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="SI2008">{{Cite news
 | title = MIT, The Chesonis Family Foundation Launch The Solar Revolution Project
 | magazine = Solar Industry
 | url = http://solarindustrymag.com/mit-the-chesonis-family-foundation-launch-the-solar-revolution-project
 | date = April 22, 2008 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web
 | title = MIT, Chesonis Foundation announce solar revolution
 | publisher = Massachusetts Institute of Technology
 | newspaper = MIT News
 | url = http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2008/chesonis-0422.html
 | date = April 22, 2008 | access-date = August 3, 2008
}}</ref> He became a co-director of the Eni Solar Frontiers Center at MIT when it was created on July 7, 2008.<ref name="ENI">{{Cite web
 |title=The "Eni Solar Frontiers Center" at MIT founded today
 |website=ENI
 |url=http://www.eni.com/en_IT/media/press-releases/2008/07/2008-07-07eni-solar.shtml
 |date=July 7, 2008
 |access-date=April 6, 2016
 |url-status=dead
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160419002000/http://www.eni.com/en_IT/media/press-releases/2008/07/2008-07-07eni-solar.shtml
 |archive-date=April 19, 2016
 |df=mdy
}}</ref>

In February 2012, Nocera agreed to move his research group to the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts,<ref name="Colen">{{Cite news
 | title = Clean energy pioneer brings lab to Harvard
 | last1 = Colen | first1 = B. D.
 | newspaper = Harvard Gazette
 | url = http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2012/03/clean-energy-pioneer-brings-lab-to-harvard/
 | date = March 8, 2012 | access-date = April 5, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="Johnson">{{Cite news
 | title = MIT energy researcher moving to Harvard
 | last1 = Johnson | first1 = Carolyn Y.
 | work = Boston Globe
 | url = https://www.bostonglobe.com/news/science/2012/03/09/mit-energy-researcher-moving-harvard/5EdmuK94b27OHUkgjwQL4L/story.html
 | date = March 9, 2012 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref> where he became the Patterson Rockwood Professor of Energy.<ref name="Colen" />

Nocera's major areas of interest are in biological and chemical energy conversion, focusing on mechanisms at the molecular level and the photogeneration of hydrogen and oxygen.<ref name="Bioinspired">{{Cite book
 | title = Bioinspired chemistry for energy : a workshop summary to the Chemical Sciences Roundtable
 | chapter = Biographies
 | edition = Biographies
 | publisher = National Academies Press | location = Washington, D.C.
 | url = https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK4087/
 | date = 2008
 | isbn = 978-0-309-11487-5
}}</ref> His work on [[artificial photosynthesis]] grows out of his basic research into mechanisms of energy conversion in biology and chemistry, particularly those involving multielectron excited states and [[proton coupled electron transfer]] (PCET).<ref name="Nocera1995">{{cite journal
| last1=Nocera|first1=Daniel G.
| title=Chemistry of the Multielectron Excited State
| journal=Accounts of Chemical Research
| date=May 1995|volume=28|issue=5
| pages=209–217
| doi=10.1021/ar00053a002}}</ref><ref name="Reece2006">{{Cite journal
 | title = Proton-coupled electron transfer: the mechanistic underpinning for radical transport and catalysis in biology.
 | last1 = Reece | first1 = SY
 | last2 = Hodgkiss | first2 = JM
 | last3 = Stubbe | first3 = J
 | last4 = Nocera | first4 = DG
 | journal = [[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B]]
| volume = 361 | issue = 1472 | pages = 1351–64
 | date = August 29, 2006 | pmid = 16873123 | doi=10.1098/rstb.2006.1874 | pmc=1647304
}}</ref><ref name="Nocera2009">{{cite journal
| last1=Nocera|first1=Daniel G.
| title=Chemistry of Personalized Solar Energy
| journal=Inorganic Chemistry
| date=2 November 2009
| volume=48|issue=21|pages=10001–10017
| doi=10.1021/ic901328v|pmc=3332084|pmid=19775081}}</ref><ref name="Troian-Gautier">{{cite journal
| last1=Troian-Gautier|first1=Ludovic
| last2=Moucheron|first2=Cécile
| title=RutheniumII Complexes bearing Fused Polycyclic Ligands: From Fundamental Aspects to Potential Applications
| journal=Molecules
| date=22 April 2014
| volume=19|issue=4|pages=5028–5087
| doi=10.3390/molecules19045028|pmid=24759069
|pmc=6270827
|doi-access=free
}}</ref><ref name="Liddle">{{cite book
| last1=Liddle|first1=Stephen T.
| title=Molecular Metal-Metal Bonds: Compounds, Synthesis, Properties
| date=6 May 2015
| publisher=John Wiley & Sons
| isbn=978-3-527-33541-1
| pages=303–304|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1iXPBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA303}}</ref>

Nocera argues that a better understanding of the [[photosynthesis]] process is essential to the development of energy strategies, because [[solar energy]] has the potential to scale up to meet long-term energy demands. He emphasizes that scientists must consider the economics of the materials they propose to use for energy sources and for storage technologies, if they are to develop viable energy alternatives.<ref name="Bullis2007">{{Cite news
 | title = Supplying the World's Energy Needs with Light and Water (Interview)
 | last1 = Bullis | first1 = Kevin
 | magazine = [[MIT Technology Review]]
 | publisher = [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]
 | url = https://www.technologyreview.com/s/407884/supplying-the-worlds-energy-needs-with-light-and-water/
 | date = May 9, 2007 | access-date = April 5, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="Kostigen">{{Cite news
 | title = Time to settle on one green path
 | last1 = Kostigen | first1 = Thomas
 | work = Market Watch
 | url = http://www.marketwatch.com/story/how-green-energy-efforts-wasting-energy
 | date = April 3, 2009 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref>

=== Multielectron excited states ===
Nocera's early work on two-electron bonds and multielectron excited states is considered to have established new paradigms in excited-state chemistry.<ref name="APS2006" /> The idea behind two-electron mixed-valency is that single-electron mixed-valence compounds and two-electron mixed-valence compounds may be analogous: single-electron mixed-valence compounds may react in one-electron steps, while two-electron mixed-valence compounds may react in two-electron steps.<ref name="Rosenthal">{{cite journal|last1=Rosenthal|first1=Joel|last2=Bachman|first2=Julien|last3=Dempsey|first3=Jillian L.|last4=Esswein|first4=Arthur J.|last5=Gray|first5=Thomas G.|last6=Hodgkiss|first6=Justin M.|last7=Manke|first7=David R.|last8=Luckett|first8=Thomas D.|last9=Pistorio|first9=Bradford J.|last10=Veige|first10=Adam S.|last11=Nocera|first11=Daniel G.|title=Oxygen and hydrogen photocatalysis by two-electron mixed-valence coordination compounds|journal=Coordination Chemistry Reviews|date=July 2005|volume=249|issue=13–14|pages=1316–1326|doi=10.1016/j.ccr.2005.03.034|url=https://www.scopus.com/record/display.uri?eid=2-s2.0-23044517194&origin=inward&txGid=0|access-date=7 April 2016|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Further, a two-electron bond can be predicted to give rise to four multielectronic states.<ref name="APS2006" /><ref name="Cotton">{{cite journal|last1=Cotton|first1=F. Albert|last2=Nocera|first2=Daniel G.|title=The Whole Story of the Two-Electron Bond, with the δ Bond as a Paradigm|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|date=July 2000|volume=33|issue=7|pages=483–490|doi=10.1021/ar980116o|pmid=10913237|url=http://www.craftychemist.net/inorganic/wp-content/uploads/2010/03/for-delta-bond-picture.pdf|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref> Nocera and his lab have extensively studied the excited states of metal complexes and clusters.<ref name="Zwitterionic">{{Cite journal
 | title = Direct Spectroscopic Detection of a Zwitterionic Excited State
 | last1 = Engebretson | first1 = D. S.
 | last2 = Zaleski | first2 = J. M.
 | last3 = Leroi | first3 = G. E.
 | last4 = Nocera | first4 = D. G.
 | journal = Science
 | year = 1994 | volume = 265 | issue = 5173 | pages = 759–762
 | doi = 10.1126/science.265.5173.759 | pmid = 17736272
| bibcode = 1994Sci...265..759E| s2cid = 46019104 }}</ref> ''Two Photon Excitation Spectrum of a Twisted Quadruple Bond Metal−Metal Complex'' completed the description of the four requisite states for the prototypical quadruple bond of a transition metal complex.<ref name="APS2006" /><ref name="Engebretson">{{cite journal
| last1=Engebretson|first1=Daniel S.
| last2=Graj|first2=Evan M.
| last3=Leroi|first3=George E.
| last4=Nocera|first4=Daniel G.
| title=Two Photon Excitation Spectrum of a Twisted Quadruple Bond Metal−Metal Complex
| journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society
| date=February 1999|volume=121|issue=4
| pages=868–869
| doi=10.1021/ja983295d
|bibcode=1999JAChS.121..868E
}}</ref>

Building on the ideas of two-electron mixed-valency, Heyduk and Nocera developed a light-driven molecular photocatalyst.  The absorption of light caused the two RhII-X bonds of a dirhodium compound to break, resulting in an active [[rhodium]] catalyst which was able to react with hydrohalic acids.<ref name="Troian-Gautier" /> Their 2001 report on the generation of H<sub>2</sub> from halohalic acid using a molecular photocatalyst is considered to have "opened the door" to photocatalytic production of fuels.<ref name="APS2006" /><ref name="Bioinspired" /><ref name="Heyduk">{{cite journal
| last1=Heyduk|first1=AF
| last2=Nocera|first2=DG
| title=Hydrogen produced from hydrohalic acid solutions by a two-electron mixed-valence photocatalyst.
| journal=Science
| date=31 August 2001
| volume=293|issue=5535
| pages=1639–41
| pmid=11533485|doi=10.1126/science.1062965|bibcode=2001Sci...293.1639H|s2cid=35989348
}}</ref>

=== The artificial leaf ===
In 2008, Nocera and [[postdoctoral]] [[fellow]] [[Matthew Kanan]] were believed to have taken an important step towards [[artificial photosynthesis]], when they created an anode electrocatalyst for the oxidation of water, capable of splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen gases.<ref name="bullis2008" /><ref name="Kleiner">{{Cite web
 | title = Electrode lights the way to artificial photosynthesis
 | last = Kleiner | first = Kurt
 | publisher = Reed Business Information
 | magazine = [[New Scientist]]
 | url = https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn14441
 | access-date = January 10, 2012
}}</ref> Their catalyst used [[cobalt]] and [[phosphate]], relatively inexpensive and easily obtainable materials.<ref name="bullis2008">{{Cite news
 | title = Solar-Power Breakthrough
 | last = Bullis | first = Kevin
 | magazine = [[MIT Technology Review]]
 | publisher = [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]
 | url = http://www.technologyreview.com/Energy/21155/page1/
 | date = July 31, 2008 | access-date = August 3, 2008
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal
 | title = In Situ Formation of an Oxygen-Evolving Catalyst in Neutral Water Containing Phosphate and Co2+
 | last1 = Kanan | first1 = M. W.
 | last2 = Nocera | first2 = D. G.
 | journal = Science
 | year = 2008 | volume = 321 | issue = 5892 | pages = 1072–1075
 | doi = 10.1126/science.1162018 | pmid = 18669820
| bibcode = 2008Sci...321.1072K| s2cid = 206514692 }}</ref><ref name="Trafton">{{Cite web
 | title = 'Major discovery' from MIT primed to unleash solar revolution
 | last = Trafton
 | first = Anne
 | publisher = [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]
 | newspaper = MIT News
 | url = http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2008/oxygen-0731.html
 | access-date = January 10, 2012
 | archive-date = March 28, 2014
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140328205311/http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2008/oxygen-0731.html
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref> The catalyst was able to split water into oxygen and protons using sunlight, and could potentially be coupled to a hydrogen gas producing catalyst such as platinum. Although the catalyst broke down during catalysis, it could repair itself.<ref name="Lutterman">{{Cite journal
 | title = A Self-Healing Oxygen-Evolving Catalyst
 | last1 = Lutterman | first1 = Daniel A.
 | author2-last = Surendranath | author2-first = Yogesh
 | author3-last = Nocera | author3-first = Daniel G.
 | journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society
 | year = 2009 | volume = 131 | issue = 11 | pages = 3838–3839
 | doi = 10.1021/ja900023k | pmid = 19249834
| bibcode = 2009JAChS.131.3838L }}</ref>

In 2009, Nocera formed Sun Catalytix, a startup to develop a prototype design for a system to convert sunlight into storable hydrogen which could be used to produce electricity. Such a system would require both technological and commercial breakthroughs to create economically viable components for hydrogen storage, solar panels, and fuel cells.<ref name="LaMonica2009">{{Cite news
 | title = MIT spin-off stores sun's energy to power the world
 | last1 = LaMonica | first1 = Martin
 | work = CNET
 | url = http://www.cnet.com/news/mit-spin-off-stores-suns-energy-to-power-the-world/
 | date = September 29, 2009 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="Jayakumar">{{Cite news
 | title = Energy start-up that created 'artificial leaf' is acquired by Lockheed Martin
 | last1 = Jayakumar | first1 = Amrita
 | newspaper = The Washington Post
 | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/capital-business/wp/2014/08/29/energy-start-up-that-developed-artificial-leaf-is-acquired-by-lockheed-martin/
 | date = August 29, 2014 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref> In October 2010, Nocera signed with the [[Tata Group]] of India to further support research and development. The ideal was to create a stand-alone miniature plant capable of providing enough "personalized energy" to power a small home.
Such a device could provide power to homes in isolated areas that are currently inaccessible.<ref>{{Cite web
 | title = Tata signs up MIT energy guru for power from water
 | last = Halarnkar | first = Samar
 | website = Live Mint
 | url = http://www.livemint.com/2011/03/23001656/Tata-signs-up-MIT-energy-guru.html
 | date = March 23, 2011
}}</ref>

In 2011, Nocera and his research team announced the creation of the first practical "artificial leaf": an advanced solar cell the size of a playing card, capable of splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen with ten times the efficiency of natural photosynthesis.<ref name="artificial leaf">{{cite web|title=Press release: Debut of the first practical "artificial leaf"|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2011/march/debut-of-the-first-practical-artificial-leaf.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|language=en|date=March 27, 2011}}</ref><ref name="Reece2011">{{Cite journal
 | title = Wireless Solar Water Splitting Using Silicon-Based Semiconductors and Earth-Abundant Catalysts
 | last1 = Reece | first1 = Steven Y.
 | author2-last = Hamel | author2-first = Jonathan A.
 | author3-last = Sung | author3-first = Kimberly
 | author4-last = Jarvi | author4-first = Thomas D.
 | author5-last = Esswein | author5-first = Arthur J.
 | author6-last = Pijpers | author6-first = Joep J. H.
 | author7-last = Nocera | author7-first = Daniel G.
 | journal = Science
 | volume = 334 | issue = 6056 | pages = 645–648
 | bibcode = 2011Sci...334..645R
 | date = November 4, 2011 | doi = 10.1126/science.1209816 | pmid = 21960528
| s2cid = 12720266 }}</ref> The silicon solar cell was coated with a thin film of cobalt catalyst on one side, over a protective membrane to prevent the silicon from oxidizing, and a nickel-based catalyst on the other side, to split hydrogen from water.<ref name="McKenna2011">{{cite news|last1=McKenna|first1=Phil|title=A Greener 'Artificial Leaf'|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/423569/a-greener-artificial-leaf/|access-date=7 April 2016|work=MIT Technology Review|date=April 7, 2011}}</ref> The artificial leaf was featured in ''Time'' magazine's list of the top 50 inventions of 2011.<ref name="Grossman">{{cite magazine|last1=Grossman|first1=Lev|last2=Thompson|first2=Mark|last3=Kluger|first3=Jeffrey|last4=Park|first4=Alice|last5=Walsh|first5=Bryan|last6=Suddath|first6=Claire|last7=Dodds|first7=Eric|last8=Webley|first8=Kayla|last9=Rawlings|first9=Nate|last10=Sun|first10=Feifei|last11=Brock-Abraham|first11=Cleo|last12=Carbone|first12=Nick|title=The 50 Best Inventions|url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,2099708,00.html|access-date=7 April 2016|magazine=Time |date=November 28, 2011}}</ref>

However, in May 2012, Sun Catalytix stated that it would not be scaling up the prototype. The predominant determiner of its cost, the construction of the photovoltaic infrastructure, was still considered too expensive to displace existing energy sources.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | title = 'Artificial leaf' faces economic hurdle | department = News & Comment
 | author = Richard Van Noorden
 | journal = Nature
 | url = http://www.nature.com/news/artificial-leaf-faces-economic-hurdle-1.10703
 | access-date = November 7, 2012
| doi = 10.1038/nature.2012.10703
 | year = 2012
 | doi-access = free
 | url-access = subscription
 }}</ref><ref name="Howes">{{Cite news
 | title = Artificial leaf in the shade but still growing
 | last1 = Howes | first1 = Laura
 | work = Chemistry World
 | url = http://www.rsc.org/chemistryworld/2013/07/artificial-leaf-synthetic-photosynthesis
 | date = July 25, 2013 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref> Nocera was reportedly "daunted by the challenges of bringing the technology to market."<ref name="McKenna" /> Nonetheless, researchers at Harvard and elsewhere continue to investigate the possibilities of the artificial leaf, looking for ways to reduce costs and increase efficiency.<ref name="McKenna">{{Cite news
 | title = New life for the artificial leaf?
 | last1 = McKenna | first1 = Phil
 | work = Ensia
 | url = http://ensia.com/features/new-life-for-the-artificial-leaf/
 | date = November 17, 2014 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="Hitt">{{Cite news
 | title = The Artificial Leaf Is Here. Again.
 | last1 = Hitt | first1 = Jack
 | newspaper = [[The New York Times]]
 | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/30/technology/the-artificial-leaf-is-here-again.html?_r=0
 | date = March 29, 2014 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref>

=== Low-cost flow battery ===
In hopes of developing a product that could be more rapidly brought to market, Sun Catalytix refocused its business model on developing a low-cost rechargeable flow battery for use in grid-scale and commercial-scale storage.<ref name="Kanellos">{{Cite news
 | title = MIT Curse Part II: Lockheed Martin Scoops Up Sun Catalytix
 | last1 = Kanellos | first1 = Michael
 | magazine = [[Forbes]]
 | url = https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaelkanellos/2014/08/26/mit-curse-part-ii-lockheed-martin-scoops-up-sun-catalytix/
 | date = August 26, 2014 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="LaMonica2013">{{Cite news
 | title = Sun Catalytix Seeks Second Act with Flow Battery
 | last1 = LaMonica | first1 = Martin
 | magazine = MIT Technology Review
 | url = https://www.technologyreview.com/s/512071/sun-catalytix-seeks-second-act-with-flow-battery/
 | date = March 5, 2013 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref> In 2014, Sun Catalytix was acquired by [[Lockheed Martin]], because it was interested in using the flow battery in its microgrid.<ref name="Jayakumar" /><ref name="Kanellos" /><ref name="Young">{{Cite news
 | title = Lockheed Martin Buys MIT-Spinoff Sun Catalytix After It Reinvents Itself
 | last1 = Young | first1 = Angelo
 | website = [[International Business Times]]
 | url = http://www.ibtimes.com/lockheed-martin-buys-mit-spinoff-sun-catalytix-after-it-reinvents-itself-1668202
 | date = August 25, 2014 | access-date = April 6, 2016
}}</ref><ref name="bbc" />

=== Proton-coupled electron transfer ===
The other area in which Nocera is considered a pioneer is proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET).  While he did not originate the idea that electron transfer and proton transfer could be studied as coupled processes, he published one of the foundational papers demonstrating a model for such study in 1992.<ref name="APS2006" /><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Turró | first1 = C | last2 = Chang | first2 = CK | last3 = Leroi | first3 = GE | last4 = Cukier | first4 = RI | last5 = Nocera | first5 = DG | year = 1992 | title = Photoinduced electron transfer mediated by a hydrogen-bonded interface | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc. | volume = 114 | issue = 10| pages = 4013–4015 | doi=10.1021/ja00036a081| bibcode = 1992JAChS.114.4013T }}</ref> Using Zn porphyrin as a donor and 3,4- dinitrobenzoic acid as an acceptor, his team demonstrated photoexcitation of the Zn porphyrin and an electron transfer process utilizing a [[hydrogen bond]].  This also illustrated the viability of the approach as a model for studying biological energy conversion.<ref name="APS2006" /> PCET has become an important technique for studying energy conversion in biological processes at the molecular level.<ref name="APS2006" /><ref name="PCET2009">{{cite journal|last1=Reece|first1=Steven Y.|last2=Nocera|first2=Daniel G.|title=Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer in Biology: Results from Synergistic Studies in Natural and Model Systems|journal=Annual Review of Biochemistry|date=June 2009|volume=78|issue=1|pages=673–699|doi=10.1146/annurev.biochem.78.080207.092132|pmc=4625787|pmid=19344235}}</ref>

=== Other research ===
Other contributions include synthesis of an S = 1/2 [[kagome lattice]], of interest to the study of [[Geometrical frustration|spin-frustrated systems]] and conduction mechanisms in [[superconductors]];<ref name="Shores">{{cite journal|last1=Shores|first1=Matthew P.|last2=Nytko|first2=Emily A.|last3=Bartlett|first3=Bart M.|last4=Nocera|first4=Daniel G.|title=A Structurally Perfect S=1/2 Kagomé Antiferromagnet|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=October 2005|volume=127|issue=39|pages=13462–13463|doi=10.1021/ja053891p|pmid=16190686|bibcode=2005JAChS.12713462S }}</ref> development of [[microfluidic]] optical [[Molecular sensor|chemosensors]] for use on the microscale and nanoscale;<ref name="Rudzinski">{{cite journal|last1=Rudzinski|first1=Christina M.|last2=Young|first2=Albert M.|last3=Nocera|first3=Daniel G.|title=A Supramolecular Microfluidic Optical Chemosensor|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|date=February 2002|volume=124|issue=8|pages=1723–1727|doi=10.1021/ja010176g|pmid=11853449|bibcode=2002JAChS.124.1723R }}</ref><ref name="Demchenko">{{cite book|last1=Demchenko|first1=Alexander P.|title=Introduction to Fluorescence Sensing|date=2010|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-90-481-8049-3|pages=391–394|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wMARxPxkE7EC&pg=PA391}}</ref>
and [[molecular tagging velocimetry]] (MTV) techniques.<ref>{{Cite web
 | title = Molecular Tagging Velocimetry (MTV)
 | year = 2005
 | publisher = [[Michigan State University]]
 | url = http://www.egr.msu.edu/tmual/MTV.html
 | access-date = August 3, 2008
}}</ref>

Nocera has published over 225 [[Academic publishing|papers]].<ref name="C&EN" /><ref name="Publications">{{Cite web
 | title = Publications by year
 | publisher = Harvard University
 | website = Nocera Lab
 | url = http://nocera.harvard.edu/Publications2010
 | access-date = April 5, 2016
 | archive-date = March 29, 2016
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160329010305/http://nocera.harvard.edu/Publications2010
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref> He is a co-editor of ''Photochemistry and Radiation Chemistry'' (1998).<ref name="Wishart">{{Cite book
 | title = Photochemistry and Radiation Chemistry (Advances in Chemistry Series)
 | last = Wishart | first = James F.
 | author2 = Daniel G. Nocera
 | year = 1998
 | publisher = American Chemical Society
 | isbn = 978-0-8412-3499-4
}}</ref> He has served on scientific advisory boards and editorial boards of several large corporations.  He was the inaugural editor of ''[[List of scientific journals in chemistry|Inorganic Chemistry Communications]]'',<ref name="APS2006">{{cite journal|title=2006 I-APS Awards|journal=I-APS Newsletter|date=2006|volume=28
| pages=11–14|url=http://www.i-aps.org/newsletters/2006.pdf|access-date=7 April 2016}}</ref> and was the inaugural chair of the editorial board for ''ChemSusChem''.<ref name="ChemSusChem">{{cite journal|last1=Nocera|first1=Daniel G.|title=Great Challenges Ahead|journal=ChemSusChem|date=22 February 2008|volume=1|issue=1–2|pages=8|doi=10.1002/cssc.200800010|pmid=18605660|bibcode=2008ChSCh...1....8N }}</ref>

== Controversy and allegations ==
In 2026, allegations surfaced that Harvard chemist Daniel Nocera was aware of the sexual harassment of a PhD student by his then-student, Kwabena Bediako, during their time at Harvard in 2017. Reports at the time alleged that Nocera failed to take significant disciplinary or corrective action following the disclosure.<ref name="ChemWorld2026">{{cite news |last1= |first1= |title=UC Berkeley chemistry professor accused of sexual harassment |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/news/uc-berkeley-chemistry-professor-accused-of-sexual-harassment/4023367.article |work=[[Chemistry World]] |date=2026 |access-date=May 20, 2026}}</ref> Following the public emergence of the controversy, Nocera's invitation to deliver the Seaborg Lectures at UC Berkeley's College of Chemistry was postponed without an officially stated reason.<ref name="ChemWorld2026" />

Nocera has unequivocally denied the allegations, issuing a statement asserting that he would never act with levity or be cavalier when presented with claims of sexual harassment.<ref name="ChemWorld2026" /> He further stated, "These and any other allegations against me are defamatory and provably false, and if necessary, I will prove it in court."<ref name="ChemWorld2026" />
